tagline.text: A roughly 30 m waterfall in the Magpet forest on the slopes of Mount Apo, with a warm kawa-kawa bath above

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Tamiling, Barangay Bongolanon, Magpet, Cotabato

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (avoid right after heavy rain and landslide-prone periods)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~900 (round-trip motorcycle from Kidapawan, entrance fees and snacks, per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Davao International Airport (DVO) or Cotabato Airport (CBO)

children.text: Tausuvan Falls is a waterfall about 30 m high in Barangay Bongolanon, Magpet, Cotabato, on the slopes of Mount Apo. Close to Kidapawan and easy to reach, it is the most popular of the falls in the area, and you can enjoy both the cold plunge pool and a warm kawa-kawa bath above it.

Tausuvan Falls lies in Sitio Tamiling, Barangay Bongolanon, in the municipality of Magpet, Cotabato. The spelling varies from source to source: it also appears as Tousuvan, Tawsuvan and Bongolanon Falls. Even if the name looks slightly different on Google Maps or on a signboard, all of these point to the same place. It sits on the northern slopes of
Mount Apo
, in forest about
2.5km
east of Bongolanon village on the map. Locals sometimes call the area Sitio Waterfall, after the falls.
Travel writers present this as the most popular and most accessible of the falls on the Mount Apo foothills. The height of the drop is given as anywhere from about
to
, and both a 2014 MindaNews article and a 2024 travel blog say about

. The water collects in a natural pool at the base. Because it comes straight down from the mountain, it is very cold even at midday, and one blogger wrote that it was hard to stay in for long. Most visitors therefore dip their feet or cool off briefly. What sets this place apart is the kawa-kawa bath upstairs. Kawa-kawa means a large cauldron, and if you walk up above the falls you will find a wide bathing area where the water is not cold. If you are chilled from the pool below, moving up there to warm up is half the fun of the visit. A 2021 blog listed the kawa-kawa bath as a separate
fee, so confirm the current rate on site.

The area around the falls is known as ancestral land of the Bagobo indigenous community. A 2014 article reported about 72 households in the village, mostly Bagobo, and a 2020 GMA report said entrance revenue is shared among the barangay, the province, the Magpet municipal government, the indigenous peoples' representative and the tribal council. Residents earn a living as porters, guides and motorcycle drivers, so it is reassuring to think of entrance and service fees as money that goes to the local community. You should also know that the terrain here is unstable. After the series of earthquakes that shook Cotabato in late October 2019, a landslide damaged the entrance and cracked the ground, and as of a January 2020 GMA report the falls were temporarily closed for rehabilitation and the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) was reported to have designated the area landslide-prone (this is confirmed by that single report only). It later reopened, but in June 2024 heavy rain again blocked the entrance with mud and debris, the barangay temporarily closed the main entrance, and camping and overnight stays were restricted at that time. The falls draw an average of about 150 people on an ordinary day and close to 800 on weekends, making them one of the busiest attractions in the area. On any given day the road or the falls area may be closed, so before you set out, ask the Magpet municipal tourism office or the barangay whether it is currently open.

A half day from Kidapawan is enough. The ride itself is short, but the road above the village is narrow and rough, and its condition changes a lot when it rains. Many visitors combine the falls with the Lake Agko hot spring farther along the same road for a one-day trip. If it is your first visit, start early, see the falls before lunch, warm up in the kawa-kawa, and head back down.

blocks.title: A roughly 30 m waterfall and its natural pool

children.text: Water drops from a rock face in the forest into a pool at the base. The water is very cold, so long swims are hard; most people dip their feet or take photos in the spray. The volume varies greatly with the weather.

Walking up above the falls, you will find a wide bathing area where the water is not cold. It is a good place to get in when you have cooled down at the bottom of the falls. A separate fee may apply, so ask at the entrance.
The walk from the ecopark parking area to the falls takes about
20 minutes
and is mostly stairs. One travel blog put the climb back to the parking area at about 100 steps. The return is uphill, so expect to be out of breath.

blocks.title: Cool air at about 1,036 m above sea level

children.text: The area around the ecopark is described as about
above sea level, cooler than the lowlands and pleasantly chilly in the morning and evening. One blog even mentions the water dropping to around 6℃ at night. A long-sleeved layer is a good idea.
The ecopark has cottages where families can sit and rest, a restroom and a lawn. Day-use cottages carry a separate usage fee. On crowded weekends, spots fill up quickly.
A local information post from September 2025 lists tent camping at ₱50. In heavy rain, however, camping and overnight stays can be blocked, so ask in advance. Nights get quite cold.

blocks.title: Meeting the village and indigenous culture

children.text: Bongolanon is a mountain village where Bagobo residents live. Ask your guide or motorcycle driver about the village, and they will also point out the way safely. When taking photos, ask residents for permission first.

items.title: Half-day course from Kidapawan
items.subtitle: The falls and the kawa-kawa bath

children.text: In Kidapawan town, take a jeepney or a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) toward the Kidapawan–Magpet road. The usual way is a jeepney as far as Ginatilan, then habal-habal the rest of the way to the village. Ask locally for the best route.
At the village entrance, pay the road entrance fee and the falls entrance fee and sign the logbook. The fees are around
and
From the ecopark parking area, follow the staircase path down to the falls. It takes about
20 minutes
Take photos in front of the falls and dip your feet. The water is very cold, so do not stay in long.
Climb above the falls to the kawa-kawa bath and warm up.
Eat the lunch you brought at a cottage and rest. The stairs back are uphill, so leave yourself time.
Climb back to the parking area and return to Kidapawan. It is safer to leave the village before rain starts.
After dark the mountain road is dim, and rain can turn the road into a stream, so plan to be down by 3 p.m. at the latest.

items.title: One-day course combined with Lake Agko
items.subtitle: Waterfall and hot spring

children.text: Leave Kidapawan and head up the road toward Lake Agko first. Many blogs say the falls and the lake hot spring are on the same road.
At Tausuvan Falls, enjoy the falls and the kawa-kawa bath.
Have lunch nearby and move on toward the Lake Agko hot spring. Agree the travel time and fare with your motorcycle driver beforehand.
Come back down to Kidapawan before dark.
Covering both places in one day means more travel, so pick a day with good weather.
There are nonstop flights from Manila (NAIA) to Davao International Airport (DVO). Check the airline's latest timetable for frequency and times.
Cotabato Airport (CBO) is another option, but you would still need to continue overland to Kidapawan, so Davao is usually more convenient.
Buses and vans run from Davao toward Kidapawan. Check the schedule and fare at the terminal.
From Kidapawan town to the falls village is described as about
20~30 minutes
, but it can take longer depending on the road.
By car, head south along the Kidapawan–Magpet road, turn left at Ginatilan, and go through Kisandal to Bongolanon. The road is mostly paved but has narrow, uneven stretches.
By public transport, take a jeepney to Ginatilan, then switch to habal-habal for Kisandal and Bongolanon.
A 2021 blog said the habal-habal fare from Kidapawan town was about ₱80, and that this fare also covered Lake Agko. Negotiate the current fare with the driver.
The last stretch is steep and slippery when it rains. A 2014 article tells of a van that could not climb it, so its passengers walked up.
The area can be visited year-round, but it is easily affected by landslides and heavy rain. Right after heavy rain the entrance road has been blocked or closed before, so check the weather first.
We could not confirm seasonal weather from the sources, so the table below gives only general guidance. Check the forecast and local advice before you go.

There are no large lodgings in the falls village. To stay overnight, you can pitch a tent at the ecopark or rent a cottage, but camping has been restricted during heavy rain, so check ahead. Most travelers stay in Kidapawan town and visit as a day trip.

A 2014 article mentions a service that cooked native chicken for visitors. We cannot tell whether that is still the case, so it is best to bring food and water from Kidapawan. Take your trash back with you.
Agree on the round-trip and waiting fare with your motorcycle driver before you set off.
The falls water is very cold, so bring a towel, a change of clothes and a light jacket.
There are many stairs, so shoes with good grip are best. Sandals are not recommended.
Carry small bills. Entrance fees and the kawa-kawa fee are mostly paid in cash.
There is a logbook to sign, so please cooperate even if it feels like a bother.
Going on a weekday morning rather than a weekend is far quieter.
Phone signal may be weak, so save your route beforehand.
Check the latest announcements. Fees and opening status change often.
This area has been designated landslide-prone, and the entrance has closed after earthquakes and heavy rain. Be sure to confirm that it is open before you leave.
Do not go on rainy days or right afterward, as paths are slippery and landslides are a risk.
The falls water is very cold, and staying in too long carries a risk of hypothermia.
Stairs and rocks are slippery, so walk slowly.
This is indigenous ancestral land, so follow local guidance and leave no trash.
Camping can be prohibited depending on the weather.
Magpet, where the falls are, lies on the foothills of Mount Apo. Summit trails have been closed in some areas, so check the latest announcements.
A lake hot spring farther along the same road, often visited together with the falls. Check travel time and road conditions locally.
The city where flights from Manila arrive. From there you continue overland to Kidapawan.
